stem: Which keyword is used for a class to inherit from another class?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: "inherits" is not a Java keyword.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: extends is used to declare that one class inherits from another.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: "implements" is used for interfaces, not for extending a class.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: "super" refers to the superclass from within a subclass; it's not used for declaring inheritance in the class header.

explanation: `extends` is the keyword used to declare that a class inherits from another class.

stem: In `public class Dog extends Animal`, which class is the superclass?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Dog is the subclass, the one doing the extending.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Animal is being extended, making it the superclass.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Only one of these is the superclass; Dog is the subclass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither; there is no superclass here
choices.explanation: Animal is indeed acting as the superclass, since Dog extends it.

explanation: In `Dog extends Animal`, `Animal` is the superclass and `Dog` is the subclass.

stem: What does a subclass automatically inherit from its superclass?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Private fields are NOT directly accessible/inherited in the usual sense from outside the declaring class, even by subclasses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A subclass does not inherit the superclass's constructors; it can only call them via super().

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public and protected fields and methods (not private ones)
choices.explanation: Inheritance gives a subclass access to the superclass's non-private members.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance genuinely gives the subclass access to non-private members of the superclass.

explanation: A subclass inherits its superclass's public and protected fields and methods, but not private ones.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Dog inherits eat() from Animal automatically, so calling it prints "eating".

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Dog inherits eat() from Animal automatically, even without defining it itself.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is valid; Dog can call any public method inherited from Animal.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: eat() actually executes and prints "eating"; it doesn't return anything that would be null.

explanation: `Dog` inherits `eat()` from `Animal`, so `d.eat()` prints `"eating"`.

stem: Can a Java class extend more than one class directly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes, using commas to list multiple superclasses
choices.explanation: Java does not allow a class to extend multiple classes using commas; that would be multiple inheritance, which Java doesn't support for classes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, Java only supports single inheritance for classes (one direct superclass)
choices.explanation: Every Java class can extend at most one other class directly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, but only up to 3 classes
choices.explanation: There's no such "up to 3" rule; Java strictly allows exactly one direct superclass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only if the classes are in the same package
choices.explanation: Being in the same package doesn't change this rule; single inheritance applies universally to classes.

explanation: Java supports only single inheritance for classes -- a class can extend exactly one direct superclass.

stem: What is the relationship implied by `public class Cat extends Animal`?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: "has-a" describes composition (an object containing another as a field), not inheritance.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Inheritance establishes an is-a relationship: a Cat is a specific kind of Animal.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This reverses the relationship; the specific subclass "is-a" more general superclass, not the other way around.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance establishes a very meaningful is-a relationship between the classes.

explanation: Inheritance models an "is-a" relationship: a `Cat` is a kind of `Animal`.

stem: If class `Animal` has a public field `name`, and `Dog extends Animal`, can code inside `Dog`'s methods directly access `name`?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, subclasses can never access superclass fields
choices.explanation: Subclasses absolutely can access inherited public (and protected) fields directly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, since name is public (and would also be accessible if it were protected)
choices.explanation: A public or protected field is directly accessible from subclass code.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only if Dog redeclares the field itself
choices.explanation: Redeclaring the field would actually create a separate, shadowing field, not access the inherited one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A getter is one way to access it, but direct access is also possible for a public or protected field.

explanation: Since `name` is public, `Dog`'s methods can access it directly through inheritance.

stem: What does `super()` do when called as the first line of a subclass constructor?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: super() does not create an entirely separate object; it initializes the superclass portion of the current object being constructed.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: super() invokes the superclass's constructor to initialize the inherited part of the object.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Calls a method named "super" in the current class
choices.explanation: super() is not a call to a method named "super"; it's special syntax for calling a superclass constructor.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Java doesn't support deleting classes, and super() has nothing to do with that.

explanation: `super()` calls the superclass's no-argument constructor to initialize the inherited portion of the object.

stem: If a subclass constructor doesn't explicitly call `super(...)`, what happens?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This doesn't always cause a compile error; Java handles the common case automatically (an error only occurs if the superclass has no accessible no-arg constructor).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Java automatically inserts a call to the superclass's no-argument constructor as the first statement
choices.explanation: Java implicitly adds a call to super() if the subclass constructor doesn't provide one explicitly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The object is created without initializing any inherited fields
choices.explanation: The automatically inserted super() call does initialize the superclass's part of the object; it's not skipped.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The subclass can be instantiated normally in this case.

explanation: Java automatically inserts an implicit `super()` call as the first statement if the constructor doesn't provide one.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This misses the automatic call to Animal's constructor, which happens first.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Java implicitly calls Animal's no-arg constructor first, printing "Animal created", then runs the rest of Dog's constructor, printing "Dog created".

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This has the order backwards; the superclass constructor always finishes running before the subclass constructor's own code executes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This misses "Dog created," which does print after the implicit super() call completes.

explanation: Java implicitly calls `Animal()` first, so `"Animal created"` prints before `"Dog created"`.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: super("bark") runs first, printing "Animal makes bark", then the rest of Dog's constructor prints "Dog created".

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The explicit super("bark") call runs first, before any code after it in Dog's constructor.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This misses "Dog created," which prints after the super() call completes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This misses "Animal makes bark," which prints first due to the super("bark") call.

explanation: `super("bark")` runs first, printing `"Animal makes bark"`, followed by `"Dog created"`.

stem: Why must `super(...)`, if used, be the first statement in a subclass constructor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It's just a stylistic convention, not a real requirement
choices.explanation: This is a strict, enforced Java language rule, not just a style guideline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The superclass portion of the object must be fully initialized before the subclass's own initialization code runs
choices.explanation: Initialization must proceed from the most general (superclass) to the most specific (subclass) part of the object.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has no particular reason; it could be placed anywhere
choices.explanation: There is a specific, important reason: initialization order must proceed from superclass to subclass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It only matters for static methods
choices.explanation: This rule is about constructors, unrelated to static methods.

explanation: Java enforces that `super(...)` be the first statement, ensuring the superclass part of the object is initialized before the subclass's own code runs.

stem: What happens if `Animal` (a superclass) has only a constructor that takes a `String` parameter, and `Dog extends Animal` provides no constructor at all?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nothing; Java provides a working default constructor for Dog automatically
choices.explanation: Java cannot provide a working automatic constructor here, since it would need to call a no-arg super() that doesn't exist.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a compile error, because Java's automatically inserted super() call needs a no-argument Animal constructor, which doesn't exist
choices.explanation: Since Animal has no no-arg constructor, the implicit super() call that Java would insert fails to compile.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dog silently ignores Animal's constructor requirement
choices.explanation: The compiler does not silently ignore this; it raises an error at compile time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It works fine at compile time but crashes at runtime
choices.explanation: This is a compile-time error, not a runtime crash; the code would never even successfully compile.

explanation: Without a no-arg constructor in `Animal`, Java's implicit `super()` call fails, causing a compile error.

stem: Given the scenario in the previous question (Animal only has a String constructor), what must Dog do to compile successfully?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Without an explicit constructor calling super with a String, the code won't compile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dog must explicitly define a constructor that calls super(someString) with an appropriate argument
choices.explanation: Providing an explicit constructor that calls the existing String-based superclass constructor resolves the issue.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Declaring Dog abstract doesn't resolve the missing no-arg superclass constructor issue.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The fix is to add a proper constructor, not to remove the inheritance relationship entirely.

explanation: Dog must define a constructor that explicitly calls `super(someString)` to satisfy Animal's only available constructor.

stem: Can a subclass constructor use both `super(...)` and initialize its own additional fields?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, a constructor can only do one or the other
choices.explanation: A constructor can absolutely do both: initialize inherited state via super(), then its own additional state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes -- call super(...) first, then initialize the subclass's own fields
choices.explanation: This is the standard pattern: initialize the superclass portion first, then the subclass's own additional fields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, but only if super() is called last
choices.explanation: super(), if called explicitly, must be the FIRST statement, not the last.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, subclasses cannot have their own fields
choices.explanation: Subclasses can absolutely declare and initialize their own additional fields beyond what they inherit.

explanation: A subclass constructor typically calls `super(...)` first, then initializes any additional fields it declares.

stem: What does it mean for a subclass to "override" a method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The subclass deletes the method from the superclass
choices.explanation: Overriding doesn't delete anything from the superclass; the original method still exists there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The subclass provides a new implementation of a method that has the same signature as one in the superclass
choices.explanation: Overriding replaces the inherited behavior with a new implementation matching the same method signature.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Overriding keeps the exact same method name and signature; it doesn't rename anything.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The subclass calls the method twice
choices.explanation: Overriding is about providing a new implementation, not about how many times a method is called.

explanation: Overriding means a subclass provides its own implementation of a method matching a superclass method's signature.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Dog overrides makeSound(), so calling it on a Dog object uses Dog's version, not Animal's.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Since d is a Dog object and Dog overrides makeSound(), Dog's version executes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Only the overriding version (Dog's) actually executes; Animal's version is not separately called here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is valid method overriding, with matching signatures.

explanation: Since `Dog` overrides `makeSound()`, calling it on a `Dog` object prints `"Bark"`.

stem: For a method to properly override a superclass method, what must match between the two?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The name alone isn't sufficient; the parameter list must also match, or it becomes overloading instead of overriding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The method name and parameter list (the signature); the return type must also be compatible
choices.explanation: Overriding requires the method's name and parameters to match exactly, with a compatible return type.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The return type alone doesn't determine overriding; the full signature (name + parameters) must match.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nothing needs to match; any method in a subclass overrides any method in the superclass
choices.explanation: Overriding requires a specific matching signature; it's not just any method matching any other.

explanation: Overriding requires the method's name and parameter list to match, with a compatible return type.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This misses the "a dog, which is " prefix that Dog's overridden method adds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a dog, which is an animal
choices.explanation: Dog's describe() calls super.describe() to get "an animal" and prepends "a dog, which is ".

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This misses the part contributed by super.describe(), which appends "an animal".

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is valid; super.describe() explicitly calls the superclass's version of the overridden method.

explanation: `super.describe()` explicitly calls Animal's version, producing `"a dog, which is an animal"`.

stem: Why might a subclass use `super.methodName()` inside its own override of that method?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Using super.methodName() is optional; many overrides fully replace the superclass's behavior with no such call.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To reuse/extend the superclass's behavior rather than completely replacing it
choices.explanation: Calling super.methodName() lets the override build on top of the original behavior instead of discarding it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has no effect and is purely decorative
choices.explanation: super.methodName() actually executes the superclass's version and can affect the overall behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It deletes the superclass's version of the method
choices.explanation: Calling super.methodName() does not delete anything; the superclass's version remains fully intact.

explanation: `super.methodName()` lets an override reuse and build upon the superclass's original behavior.

stem: Which annotation is conventionally used (though optional) to indicate a method is intended to override a superclass method?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: "@Overriding" is not a real Java annotation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: @Override is the standard annotation used to mark an intended method override.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: "@Super" is not a real Java annotation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: "@Inherited" is a real annotation, but it's used on annotation type declarations, not to mark method overrides.

explanation: `@Override` is the conventional (optional) annotation for marking an intended method override.

stem: What is the benefit of using `@Override` on a method, even though it's optional?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It makes the method run faster
choices.explanation: @Override has no effect on runtime performance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The compiler checks that the method actually overrides a superclass method, catching typos (e.g. a misspelled method name) at compile time
choices.explanation: If the annotated method doesn't actually match a superclass method's signature, the compiler reports an error, catching mistakes early.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It automatically calls the superclass method too
choices.explanation: @Override doesn't automatically call anything; it's purely a compile-time check.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It changes the method's access level
choices.explanation: @Override doesn't affect a method's access modifier (public/private/etc.).

explanation: `@Override` lets the compiler verify the method genuinely overrides a superclass method, catching mistakes like typos.

choices.explanation: This is Shape's unoverridden default, but Square overrides getArea() with its own calculation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the side length itself, not the computed area.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Square's overridden getArea() computes side * side = 4 * 4 = 16.0.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is valid, correctly overridden code.

explanation: `Square`'s overridden `getArea()` computes `side * side = 4 * 4 = 16.0`.

stem: What is polymorphism, in the context of overriding methods?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ability of a variable to hold values of different, unrelated primitive types
choices.explanation: This describes something closer to type flexibility with primitives, which isn't what polymorphism means here.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ability for a superclass-typed reference to call an overridden method and have the subclass's specific version execute
choices.explanation: Polymorphism lets code written against a superclass type automatically use each object's actual, more specific behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ability to have multiple classes with the same name
choices.explanation: Java doesn't allow multiple classes with the exact same name in the same context; that's unrelated to polymorphism.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ability to delete methods at runtime
choices.explanation: Polymorphism doesn't involve deleting methods; it's about which implementation executes.

explanation: Polymorphism allows a superclass-typed reference to invoke overridden methods, with the subclass's actual version running.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Even though a is declared with type Animal, the actual object it references is a Dog, so Dog's overridden method runs.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Java uses the object's actual runtime type (Dog) to decide which overridden method to run, not the declared type (Animal).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Only one version executes: the actual object's (Dog's) overridden method, not both.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is valid; a Dog object can be referenced by an Animal-typed variable, since Dog is-a Animal.

explanation: Even though `a` is declared as `Animal`, its actual object is a `Dog`, so the overridden `makeSound()` prints `"Bark"`.

stem: In the previous example, why does `a.makeSound()` print "Bark" even though `a` is declared as type `Animal`?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Java always uses the declared (compile-time) type to decide which method runs
choices.explanation: This is backwards; Java uses the actual runtime type of the object for overridden methods, not the declared compile-time type.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Java uses the actual (runtime) type of the object to decide which overridden method runs -- this is called dynamic method dispatch
choices.explanation: Overridden instance methods are resolved based on the object's actual type at runtime, not the reference's declared type.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is entirely predictable and well-defined behavior in Java, governed by dynamic dispatch, not chance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The declared type is changed automatically when the object is assigned
choices.explanation: The declared type of the variable a remains Animal; it doesn't change, but the method call still resolves based on the object's actual type.

explanation: This is dynamic method dispatch: overridden methods are resolved using the object's actual runtime type.

stem: Given `Animal a = new Dog();`, which of the following can `a` be used to call?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only methods declared in Animal, but the actual behavior may come from Dog's overrides
choices.explanation: The compiler restricts a to Animal's interface, while dynamic dispatch determines which actual implementation runs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any method defined anywhere in Dog, including ones not in Animal
choices.explanation: A Dog-specific method not declared (or overridden) in Animal cannot be called through an Animal-typed reference without casting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only methods defined directly in Dog, not inherited ones
choices.explanation: This is backwards; a, being declared as Animal, is restricted to Animal's interface, though overridden behavior still comes from Dog.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: a can call any method that Animal declares (inherited or overridden); it's not restricted to zero methods.

explanation: The compiler restricts calls through `a` to methods declared in `Animal`, while the actual (possibly overridden) implementation comes from the runtime type.

stem: What is the benefit of writing code like `public void feedAll(Animal[] animals)` that operates on the superclass type, rather than writing separate methods for each subclass?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: There's a substantial benefit: code reuse and flexibility across all current and future subclasses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The single method can work with any subclass of Animal (Dog, Cat, etc.) without needing to know the specific subclass in advance
choices.explanation: Writing code against the superclass type lets it work polymorphically with any current or future subclass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It makes the array store more elements
choices.explanation: Using a superclass type as the parameter doesn't affect how many elements an array can hold.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents any subclass-specific behavior from ever running
choices.explanation: Subclass-specific overridden behavior still runs correctly via dynamic dispatch, even when using the superclass type.

explanation: Writing code against the superclass type lets a single method work polymorphically with any subclass.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This ignores dynamic dispatch; each object's ACTUAL type determines which makeSound() runs, not the declared array type.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Dynamic dispatch runs each object's own overridden version: Dog's "Bark", Cat's "Meow", and Animal's own "Some sound".

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Each element is a different actual type (Dog, Cat, Animal), so each calls its own distinct override, not all the same one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is valid; an array of the superclass type can hold objects of any subclass.

explanation: Dynamic dispatch runs each object's own version of `makeSound()`: `"Bark"`, `"Meow"`, then `"Some sound"`.

stem: What does the `instanceof` operator check?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether two objects have equal field values
choices.explanation: Comparing field values is done with methods like equals(), not instanceof.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether an object is an instance of a specified class (or subclass of it)
choices.explanation: instanceof checks whether an object's actual type matches (or is a subtype of) the given class.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether a variable has been initialized
choices.explanation: instanceof checks an object's type, not whether a variable happens to be initialized.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether a method has been overridden
choices.explanation: instanceof doesn't check anything about method overriding; it's purely about object type.

explanation: `instanceof` checks whether an object is an instance of a specified class or one of its subclasses.
